question: How should the advance placement of warning signs be determined?
model_answer: Direct Answer: Advance placement of warning signs is determined by providing drivers adequate Perception-Response Time, using the distances in Table 2C-3 (based on posted or 85th-percentile speed and whether the condition requires stopping, deceleration, or lane changing) applied with engineering judgment. For temporary traffic control zones, warning signs should be placed in advance of the transition and activity areas at distances that vary with roadway type, condition, and posted speed, per Table 6B-1 — from roughly 100 feet on low-speed urban streets to ½ mile or more on freeways and expressways. All of these provisions are Guidance (recommended), not mandatory Standards. Guidance (recommended): - Warning signs should be placed so that they provide an adequate PRT; the distances contained in Table 2C-3 should be applied with engineering judgment, and the effectiveness of the placement of warning signs should be periodically evaluated under both day and night conditions. - Per Table 2C-3, advance placement distances range from 225 ft (Condition A) and 115 ft (Condition B, stop condition) at 20 mph up to 1,600 ft and 1,010 ft at 85 mph; for warning signs with less than 6-inch legend or more than four words, a minimum of 100 feet should be added to the advance placement distance to provide adequate legibility. - In TTC zones, where highway conditions permit, warning signs should be placed in advance of the transition and activity areas at varying distances depending on roadway type, condition, and posted speed; where a series of two or more advance warning signs is used, the closest sign should be placed approximately 100 feet for low-speed urban streets to 1,000 feet or more for freeways and expressways (see Table 6B-1). - On freeways and expressways, advance warning sign placement should be longer because drivers are conditioned to uninterrupted flow, extending as far as ½ mile or more. - On urban streets, the effective placement of the nearest warning sign to the TTC zone should range from 4 to 8 times the speed limit in mph, with the high end used when speeds are relatively high; with two or more signs on higher-speed streets, the advance warning area should extend a greater distance. - On rural highways, the effective placement of the first warning sign should be substantially longer—from 8 to 12 times the speed limit in mph—and the advance warning area should extend 1,500 feet or more for open highway conditions. Visual evidence: - [Image 1] Table 2C-3 shows advance placement distances by posted or 85th-percentile speed for Condition A (speed reduction/lane changing in heavy traffic) and Condition B (deceleration to listed advisory speeds), with footnotes on legibility adjustments and minimum 100-ft spacing. - [Image 2] Table 6B-1 (Warning Sign Minimum Spacing) gives A, B, and C sign-spacing dimensions by road type: 100 feet for low-speed urban, 350 feet for high-speed urban, 500 feet for rural, and 1,000/1,500/2,640 feet for expressways/freeways. - [Image 3] Page 193 shows Section 2C.04 (Placement of Warning Signs) with its Guidance on providing adequate PRT and applying Table 2C-3 with engineering judgment, together with the full Table 2C-3. - [Image 4] Page 839 shows Section 6H.02 (Position of Advance Warning Signs) Guidance that signs be placed at varying distances by roadway type, condition, and posted speed, per Table 6B-1. - [Image 5] Page 197 shows Figure 2C-2 (curve warning sign examples), whose notes reference Table 2C-3 for advance placement distance guidelines. - [Image 6] Page 812 shows Section 6B.04 (Advance Warning Area) with the Guidance on freeway/expressway, urban street (4–8 times speed limit), and rural highway (8–12 times speed limit) placement. Citations: - Section 2C.04 Guidance §5 (p.152) - Section 2C.04 Guidance §804 (p.153) - Section 6H.02 Guidance §1 (p.798) - Section 6B.04 Guidance §3 (p.771) - Section 6B.04 Guidance §4 (p.771) - Section 6B.04 Guidance §6 (p.771) - Table 2C-3 (p.152) - Table 6B-1 (p.773) - Page 193 - Page 839 - Page 197 - Page 812
gold_answer: Warning signs should be placed to provide adequate perception-response time. Table 2C-3 is an aid, but its distances should be applied with engineering judgment and can be adjusted for roadway features, other signing, and visibility.
